# Probability and Non-Probability Sampling {#sec-sampling-methods}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- Identify simple, systematic, stratified and cluster sampling.
- Explain limitations of convenience and consecutive sampling.
:::

## The idea

In **probability sampling**, the selection mechanism is specified so each eligible unit has a known, nonzero inclusion probability. Common designs include simple random, stratified, systematic and cluster sampling. **Non-probability approaches** such as convenience, purposive or consecutive sampling do not generally permit design-based inference to an entire target population without additional assumptions.

## When and how to apply it

Sample-size formulas should be matched to the sampling design and intended estimand. Stratification can change precision; clustering usually increases sampling variance when observations within clusters are positively correlated. A calculation cannot compensate for selection bias caused by convenience sampling.

## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
A researcher recruits the first 250 eligible antenatal clinic attendees; another samples names from a complete registry using a random-number generator. Compare what each sample can represent.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
Do not label consecutive recruitment as simple random sampling.
:::
